question.text: TWRR (Time-Weighted Rate of Return) differs from IRR (MWRR) in that TWRR:

answer.text: Gives more weight to periods with larger investments
Eliminates the impact of cash flow timing, measuring pure investment performance independent of capital flows
Always produces a higher return than IRR
Is only used for listed equity portfolios

explanation.text: The Logic: Time-Weighted Rate of Return (TWRR) measures investment performance independent of the timing of capital flows — it isolates how well the manager invested, regardless of when capital was contributed or withdrawn. The Money-Weighted Rate of Return (MWRR or IRR), in contrast, reflects the investor's actual cash-flow-weighted experience, where larger investments at favourable times have greater impact. The Trap: TWRR weights periods equally; it does NOT give more weight to periods with larger investments (that is MWRR). TWRR is not guaranteed to be higher than IRR, and it is applicable to any portfolio with regular valuation, not just listed equities. Note: The XIX-A workbook supports IRR/FIRR as a money-weighted return and discusses ROI, MIRR, TVPI, KS-PME, and Direct Alpha; it does not specifically define TWRR or the TWRR-vs-MWRR distinction. Treat the TWRR framing as general performance-measurement knowledge — it is also tested in NISM XXI-B (Portfolio Managers).
